statement: Let $X$ be a finite [simplicial complex](c:simplicial-complex) of dimension $n \ge 5$ that is locally PL homeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^n$ and has the homotopy type of $S^n$. Then $X$ is homeomorphic to $S^n$ by a homeomorphism that is piecewise linear except at one point.

hypotheses.text: $X$ is a finite [simplicial complex](c:simplicial-complex) of dimension $n \ge 5$.
$X$ is locally PL homeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^n$, so it is a closed [PL manifold](c:piecewise-linear-manifold).
$X$ is [homotopy equivalent](c:homotopy-equivalence) to the sphere $S^n$.

conclusion: There is a [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism) $X \to S^n$ that is piecewise linear except at one point.

proofs.name: Engulfing a handle decomposition
proofs.slogan: Engulf the two halves of a handle decomposition into balls, then read off that $X$ is a sphere away from one point.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof; the engulfing theorem and the last step rest on the cited papers. Stallings proved the case $n \ge 7$ and Zeeman extended it to $n \ge 5$.

roles.why: A finite [simplicial complex](c:simplicial-complex) has a triangulation with finite skeleta and a dual complex of known dimension.
Local PL Euclidean structure makes $X$ a closed [PL manifold](c:piecewise-linear-manifold), where skeleta and dual skeleta split $X$.
The homotopy type of $S^n$ makes $X$ $(n-1)$-connected, which is the connectivity that the engulfing theorem needs.

steps.slogan: Show that $X$ is a closed PL manifold that is $(n-1)$-connected.
steps.detail: A finite complex that is locally PL homeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact [PL manifold](c:piecewise-linear-manifold) without boundary. A [homotopy equivalence](c:homotopy-equivalence) with $S^n$ gives $\pi_i(X) = 0$ for $i < n$.

steps.slogan: Split $X$ into regular neighborhoods of a $k$-complex and of its dual $(n-k-1)$-complex.
steps.detail: Triangulate $X$ as a combinatorial manifold and take the $k$-skeleton $K$ with $2 \le k \le n-3$. The complement of a regular neighborhood of $K$ is a regular neighborhood of the dual $(n-k-1)$-skeleton $L$. Both $K$ and $L$ have dimension at most $n-3$, which needs $n \ge 5$.

steps.slogan: Engulf $K$ and then $L$ into open balls with the [engulfing](c:engulfing) theorem.
steps.detail: Stallings (codimension at least 4) and Zeeman (codimension at least 3) prove: if $(M, U)$ is $k$-connected and $K$ is a polyhedron of dimension at most $k \le n-3$, then a PL homeomorphism of $M$ moves $K$ into $U$. The $(n-1)$-connected $X$ and an open ball $U$ satisfy this for $K$ and for $L$.

steps.slogan: Show that $X$ is the union of two open PL balls.
steps.detail: The neighborhoods of $K$ and of $L$ cover $X$. After the two engulfings each lies in an open ball, so $X$ is the union of two open PL balls.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $X$ is a sphere away from one point.
steps.detail: The cited papers show that this makes $X$ minus a point PL homeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^n$. The one-point compactification then gives a [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism) $X \to S^n$ that is piecewise linear off that point.

concepts.c:simplicial-complex: The theorem starts from a finite triangulated space with skeleta of known dimension.
concepts.c:piecewise-linear-manifold: Local PL Euclidean structure lets skeleta and dual skeleta split the space.
concepts.c:homotopy-equivalence: The homotopy type of the sphere gives the connectivity that engulfing needs.
concepts.c:homeomorphism: The conclusion is a homeomorphism onto the sphere, PL off one point.
concepts.c:engulfing: Engulfing moves a low-dimensional complex into a ball by an ambient PL homeomorphism.

source.ref: J. R. Stallings, Polyhedral homotopy-spheres, Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society 66 (1960), 485-488; E. C. Zeeman, The Poincare conjecture for n >= 5, in Topology of 3-manifolds and related topics (Proc. Univ. Georgia Inst., 1961), Prentice-Hall, 1962, 198-204
source.note: Stallings proves the case n >= 7 and Zeeman, with a sharper engulfing theorem, the case n >= 5; the steps outline their common engulfing argument.

statement: Let $ABCD$ be a [parallelogram](c:parallelogram) and $P$ a point of its diagonal $AC$. The parallel to $AB$ through $P$ meets $AD$ at $E$ and $BC$ at $F$. The parallel to $AD$ through $P$ meets $AB$ at $G$ and $CD$ at $H$. Then the parallelograms $GBFP$ and $EPHD$ have equal [area](c:area).

hypotheses.text: $ABCD$ is a [parallelogram](c:parallelogram).
The point $P$ lies on the diagonal $AC$.

conclusion: The parallelograms $GBFP$ and $EPHD$ have the same [area](c:area).

proofs.name: Equal halves minus equal corners
proofs.slogan: Cut each half of the parallelogram into two corner triangles and one complement, and subtract equal areas.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. If $P = A$ or $P = C$, both complementary parallelograms are degenerate and have area $0$.

roles.why: Parallel opposite sides give the two congruent halves and the corner parallelograms around the diagonal.
A point $P$ on the diagonal makes the corner pieces triangles inside the two halves.

steps.slogan: Cut $ABCD$ along the diagonal $AC$ into two triangles of equal area.
steps.detail: Opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal, so the [triangles](c:triangle) $ABC$ and $CDA$ are congruent by three equal sides. Congruent triangles have equal [area](c:area).

steps.slogan: Split each half into two small triangles and one complementary parallelogram.
steps.detail: Because $PG$ and $BC$ are [parallel](c:parallel-lines), and $PF$ and $AB$ are parallel, triangle $ABC$ is the union of triangle $AGP$, parallelogram $GBFP$ and triangle $PFC$ without overlap. In the same way triangle $CDA$ is the union of triangle $AEP$, parallelogram $EPHD$ and triangle $PHC$.

steps.slogan: Show that $AP$ halves the parallelogram $AGPE$ and $PC$ halves $PFCH$.
steps.detail: The quadrilaterals $AGPE$ and $PFCH$ are parallelograms, since their opposite sides lie on parallel lines. A diagonal splits a parallelogram into two congruent triangles. So $[AGP] = [AEP]$ and $[PFC] = [PHC]$.

steps.slogan: Subtract the equal corner triangles from the equal halves to get equal complements.
steps.detail: The decomposition gives $[GBFP] = [ABC] - [AGP] - [PFC]$ and $[EPHD] = [CDA] - [AEP] - [PHC]$. The right sides are equal by the equal halves and the equal corners, so $[GBFP] = [EPHD]$.

concepts.c:parallelogram: The figure and its three kinds of sub-parallelograms are the objects of the proof.
concepts.c:area: Equal areas of congruent pieces are added and subtracted.
concepts.c:triangle: The diagonal and the parallels cut the figure into triangles.
concepts.c:parallel-lines: Parallel lines make the pieces parallelograms and make the cuts fit without overlap.

source.note: Euclid, Elements I.43: in any parallelogram the complements of the parallelograms about the diameter are equal.

statement: Let $ABC$ be a [triangle](c:triangle) with sides $a$, $b$, $c$ opposite $A$, $B$, $C$, semiperimeter $s$, incenter $I$ and [inradius](c:inradius) $r$. Extend the two sides at $A$ beyond $A$ by $a$, the two sides at $B$ beyond $B$ by $b$, and the two sides at $C$ beyond $C$ by $c$. The six endpoints lie on the circle with center $I$ and radius $\sqrt{r^2 + s^2}$.

hypotheses.text: $ABC$ is a nondegenerate [triangle](c:triangle) with sides $a$, $b$, $c$ and semiperimeter $s$.
The two sides at each vertex are extended through that vertex by the length of the opposite side.

conclusion: The six endpoints are [concyclic](c:concyclic-points), on the circle with center $I$ and radius $\sqrt{r^2 + s^2}$.

proofs.name: Tangent lengths of the incircle
proofs.slogan: Every endpoint lies at distance $s$ from a touch point of the incircle, so it lies at one distance from the incenter.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for a nondegenerate triangle. The same argument handles the three sides, with the touch points $D$, $E$, $F$.

roles.why: A nondegenerate [triangle](c:triangle) has an incircle, and its side lengths fix the tangent lengths.
The extension lengths $a$, $b$, $c$ add to the tangent lengths and give the constant sum $s$.

steps.slogan: Find the tangent lengths from the vertices to the [incircle](c:incircle).
steps.detail: Let the incircle touch $AB$, $BC$, $CA$ at $D$, $E$, $F$. Tangent segments from one point to a circle are equal, so $AD = AF = x$, $BD = BE = y$, $CE = CF = z$. Then $x + y = c$, $y + z = a$, $x + z = b$, which gives $x = s - a$, $y = s - b$, $z = s - c$.

steps.slogan: Measure the distance from each touch point to the two endpoints on its side.
steps.detail: On line $AB$ the endpoint beyond $A$ is $a$ from $A$, and $AD = s - a$, so it is at distance $(s - a) + a = s$ from $D$. The endpoint beyond $B$ is at distance $(s - b) + b = s$ from $D$. The same sums give distance $s$ from $E$ on $BC$ and from $F$ on $CA$.

steps.slogan: Compute each endpoint's distance from $I$ with the Pythagorean theorem.
steps.detail: The radius $ID$ is perpendicular to $AB$ and has length $r$. For an endpoint $P$ on $AB$, triangle $IDP$ has a right angle at $D$, so $IP^2 = r^2 + s^2$. The same holds on $BC$ and $CA$ with $E$ and $F$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that all six endpoints lie on one circle about $I$.
steps.detail: All six endpoints are at distance $\sqrt{r^2 + s^2}$ from $I$, so they lie on the circle with center $I$ and that radius.

concepts.c:triangle: The triangle supplies the sides, the semiperimeter and the incircle.
concepts.c:inradius: The inradius is the common height of the right triangles at the incenter.
concepts.c:incircle: Its touch points split each side into the tangent lengths.
concepts.c:concyclic-points: Equal distance from the incenter is the way to show that the points are concyclic.

source.note: The standard proof from the tangent lengths of the incircle, for the circle attributed to John H. Conway.

statement: Let $f$ be [meromorphic](c:meromorphic-function) on the closed disk $\{|z| \le R\}$ and not locally zero at any point of it. Then, off a discrete subset of the disk, $f = F\,G\,h$. Here $F = \prod_{|u|<R} \big(\tfrac{R^2 - \bar u z}{R(z-u)}\big)^{-\operatorname{div} f(u)}$, $G = \prod_{|v|=R} (z-v)^{\operatorname{div} f(v)}$, and $h$ is [analytic](c:analytic-function) near the disk and nowhere zero on it.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is [meromorphic](c:meromorphic-function) on the closed disk $\{|z| \le R\}$, with values in a complex normed space.
At every point of the disk, $f$ is not identically zero near that point.

conclusion: There is a function $h$, [analytic](c:analytic-function) near the disk and nonzero on it, with $f = F\,G\,h$ off a discrete subset of the disk.

formal.difference: The declaration allows every real $R$, with an empty disk for $R < 0$, and states the identity modulo a discrete subset of the disk, as here. The function $h$ is analytic on a neighborhood of the disk.

proofs.name: Canonical factors, then extraction
proofs.slogan: Divide out the canonical factors for the interior zeros and poles, then extract the boundary zeros and poles.
proofs.scope: The case $R > 0$. For $R < 0$ the disk is empty, and for $R = 0$ it is the point $0$ and $h$ is the trailing coefficient of $f$ at $0$, which is nonzero by the order hypothesis.

roles.why: The closed disk is compact, so $f$ has finitely many zeros and poles there and its [divisor](c:divisor) has finite support.
Finite order at each point keeps the divisor defined and the reduced function $g$ not locally zero.

steps.slogan: Divide out the canonical factors for the zeros and poles inside the open disk.
steps.detail: The canonical decomposition writes $f$, off a discrete set, as $F \cdot g$. Here $F$ is the product of the canonical factors $\frac{R^2 - \bar u z}{R(z-u)}$ to the power $-\operatorname{div} f(u)$ for $|u| < R$, where $\operatorname{div} f$ is the [divisor](c:divisor) of $f$. The function $g$ is meromorphic, in normal form, and has no zeros or poles in the open disk.

steps.slogan: Show that $g$ has finite order at every point of the closed disk.
steps.detail: At a point of the open disk, $g$ has order $0$. The closed disk is connected, and a meromorphic function in normal form with finite order at one point has finite order at every point, by the identity theorem.

steps.slogan: Match the zeros and poles of $g$ on the circle with those of $f$.
steps.detail: Near a point $v$ of the circle $|v| = R$, each canonical factor is analytic and nonzero, because $|u| < R$ gives $v \ne u$ and $R^2 - \bar u v \ne 0$. So $g$ and $f$ have the same order at $v$, and $\operatorname{div} g(v) = \operatorname{div} f(v)$. The divisor of $g$ vanishes inside the disk, so its support is a finite subset of the circle.

steps.slogan: Extract the zeros and poles of $g$ to leave an analytic factor $h$ without zeros.
steps.detail: A function that is meromorphic on the disk, has finite orders and has a finitely supported divisor equals $\prod_v (z-v)^{\operatorname{div} g(v)}$ times a function $h$. This $h$ is [analytic](c:analytic-function) near the disk and nonzero on it, off a discrete set.

steps.slogan: Combine the two factorizations of $f$ and compare the exceptional sets.
steps.detail: Substitute $g = G\,h$ into $f = F\,g$, using $\operatorname{div} g(v) = \operatorname{div} f(v)$ from the boundary step. Each factorization holds off a discrete set, and the union of two discrete sets is discrete.

concepts.c:meromorphic-function: The function and the reduced function $g$ are meromorphic on the closed disk.
concepts.c:analytic-function: The factor $h$ is analytic and has no zeros, so it carries no divisor.
concepts.c:divisor: The divisor records the orders that the canonical and boundary factors reproduce.

source.note: mathlib applies MeromorphicOn.exists_canonicalDecomp, then MeromorphicOn.extract_zeros_poles to the remaining factor, and CanonicalDecomp.divisor_eq_divisor to match the divisor on the circle.

statement: Let $ABC$ be a [triangle](c:triangle). For each side, the two [angle trisectors](c:angle-trisector) nearer to that side meet at a point. The three points so obtained are the vertices of an [equilateral triangle](c:equilateral-triangle).

hypotheses.text: $ABC$ is a nondegenerate [triangle](c:triangle) with angles $3\alpha$, $3\beta$, $3\gamma$.

conclusion: The three points form an [equilateral triangle](c:equilateral-triangle) of side $8R\sin\alpha\sin\beta\sin\gamma$, where $R$ is the circumradius.

proofs.name: Trigonometric computation
proofs.slogan: Compute two sides of the triangle of trisector points with the law of sines and cosines and see that the result is symmetric.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for the first Morley triangle formed by the trisectors that are nearer to the sides. The proof computes one side and gets the other two by relabeling.

roles.why: The angle sum $3\alpha + 3\beta + 3\gamma = 180^\circ$ gives $\alpha + \beta + \gamma = 60^\circ$, and the circumradius fixes the side lengths.

steps.slogan: Name the angles $3\alpha$, $3\beta$, $3\gamma$ and the trisector points $X$, $Y$, $Z$.
steps.detail: Since the angles of a [triangle](c:triangle) sum to $180^\circ$, $\alpha + \beta + \gamma = 60^\circ$. Let $X$ be the point of the two trisectors nearer to $BC$, and $Z$ the point of those nearer to $AB$. Triangle $BXC$ has angles $\beta$ at $B$ and $\gamma$ at $C$, and triangle $AZB$ has angles $\alpha$ at $A$ and $\beta$ at $B$.

steps.slogan: Prove the identity $\sin 3\theta = 4\sin\theta\sin(60^\circ - \theta)\sin(60^\circ + \theta)$.
steps.detail: Since $\sin(60^\circ - \theta)\sin(60^\circ + \theta) = \sin^2 60^\circ - \sin^2\theta = \tfrac34 - \sin^2\theta$, the product equals $3\sin\theta - 4\sin^3\theta = \sin 3\theta$.

steps.slogan: Compute $BX$ and $BZ$ with the law of sines and the identity.
steps.detail: The law of sines in $BXC$ gives $BX = a\sin\gamma / \sin(\beta + \gamma)$, with $a = 2R\sin 3\alpha$ and $\beta + \gamma = 60^\circ - \alpha$. The identity gives $BX = 8R\sin\alpha\sin\gamma\sin(60^\circ + \alpha)$. In the same way $BZ = 8R\sin\alpha\sin\gamma\sin(60^\circ + \gamma)$.

steps.slogan: Find $XZ$ from the law of cosines in triangle $XBZ$, where $\angle XBZ = \beta$.
steps.detail: With $K = 8R\sin\alpha\sin\gamma$ we get $XZ^2 = K^2[\sin^2(60^\circ + \alpha) + \sin^2(60^\circ + \gamma) - 2\sin(60^\circ + \alpha)\sin(60^\circ + \gamma)\cos\beta]$. The angle between the trisectors $BX$ and $BZ$ is the middle third $\beta$ of the angle at $B$.

steps.slogan: Recognize the bracket as a law of cosines for a triangle with angles $60^\circ + \alpha$, $60^\circ + \gamma$, $\beta$.
steps.detail: These three angles sum to $120^\circ + \alpha + \beta + \gamma = 180^\circ$, so they are the angles of a triangle whose sides are proportional to their sines. Its law of cosines shows that the bracket equals $\sin^2\beta$. Hence $XZ = 8R\sin\alpha\sin\beta\sin\gamma$.

steps.slogan: Repeat for the other sides and compare the three lengths.
steps.detail: The value $8R\sin\alpha\sin\beta\sin\gamma$ is symmetric in $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$, so relabeling gives $XY = YZ = ZX$. It is positive, so the points are distinct and form an equilateral triangle.

concepts.c:triangle: The triangle fixes the angles $3\alpha$, $3\beta$, $3\gamma$ and the circumradius.
concepts.c:angle-trisector: The trisectors give the angles $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$ at the base points.
concepts.c:equilateral-triangle: Three equal sides are what the computation proves.

source.note: The classical trigonometric proof of Morley's theorem, by the law of sines, the triple-angle identity and the law of cosines.

statement: Let $M$ be a [charted space](c:charted-space) over a model space $H$ with the [discrete topology](c:discrete-topology). Then $M$ is discrete. A 0-manifold is the case where $H$ is a point.

hypotheses.text: $M$ is a [charted space](c:charted-space) over $H$: every point has a chart, a homeomorphism from an open set of $M$ onto an open set of $H$.
The model space $H$ has the [discrete topology](c:discrete-topology).

conclusion: Every subset of $M$ is open, so $M$ has the discrete topology.

formal.difference: The declaration is more general than a 0-manifold: it takes any discrete model space, not only a one-point space of dimension zero. It states exactly the discreteness of $M$.

proofs.name: Singletons as chart fibers
proofs.slogan: Show that each point is isolated by pulling back an open singleton of $H$ through its chart.
proofs.scope: The whole statement, for any discrete model space $H$; a 0-manifold is the case where $H$ is a point. The empty space is discrete.

roles.why: The chart at each point is injective and continuous on an open source, which lets it carry an open singleton back to $M$.
Discreteness of $H$ makes every singleton of $H$ open.

steps.slogan: Fix a point $x$ and take its chart $\varphi$ with open source $U$.
steps.detail: The chart $\varphi$ at $x$ is a [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism) from an open set $U \ni x$ of $M$ onto an open set of $H$. In particular $\varphi$ is continuous and injective on $U$.

steps.slogan: Pull back the open singleton $\{\varphi(x)\}$ of $H$ to an open set of $M$.
steps.detail: In the discrete space $H$ every subset is [open](c:open-set), so $\{\varphi(x)\}$ is open. Since $\varphi$ is continuous on the open set $U$, the set $V = U \cap \varphi^{-1}(\{\varphi(x)\})$ is open in $M$.

steps.slogan: Show that $V = \{x\}$ because the chart is injective on its source.
steps.detail: The point $x$ lies in $V$. If $y \in V$, then $y \in U$ and $\varphi(y) = \varphi(x)$, so $y = x$ because $\varphi$ is [injective](c:injective-map) on $U$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that every singleton is open, so $M$ is discrete.
steps.detail: The point $x$ was arbitrary, so all singletons of $M$ are open. Every subset is a union of singletons, so every subset is open.

concepts.c:charted-space: Charts are the local identification with $H$ that the proof uses.
concepts.c:discrete-topology: In a discrete model space every singleton is open.
concepts.c:homeomorphism: A chart is a homeomorphism between open sets, so it is continuous and injective.
concepts.c:open-set: The proof builds an open set of $M$ that equals a single point.
concepts.c:injective-map: Injectivity of the chart on its source collapses the fiber to one point.

source.note: mathlib uses discreteTopology_iff_isOpen_singleton: the set (chartAt x).source inter chartAt x preimage of the singleton is open (isOpen_inter_preimage) and equals {x} because chartAt is injective on its source.

statement: Let $D\colon \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{Z}$ be a [divisor](c:divisor) with locally finite support and $D \ge 0$. For radii $1 \le \rho < r$, $\big(\sum_{|z| \le \rho} D(z)\big)\log\frac{r}{\rho} \le N(D, r)$. Here $N(D, r) = \sum_{0 < |z| \le r} D(z)\log\frac{r}{|z|} + D(0)\log r$ is the [logarithmic counting function](c:logarithmic-counting-function).

hypotheses.text: $D(z) \ge 0$ for every $z \in \mathbb{C}$.
The support of $D$ is locally finite, so it meets every closed disk in a finite set.
The radii satisfy $1 \le \rho < r$.

conclusion: $\big(\sum_{|z| \le \rho} D(z)\big)\log\frac{r}{\rho} \le N(D, r)$, the [logarithmic counting function](c:logarithmic-counting-function) of $D$ at radius $r$.

proofs.name: Termwise comparison
proofs.slogan: Reduce both sides to one finite sum and compare the terms one by one.
proofs.scope: The whole statement. The point $z = 0$ needs $\rho \ge 1$, because its term in $N(D, r)$ is $D(0)\log r$ and not $D(0)\log(r/|0|)$.

roles.why: Nonnegative multiplicities keep every termwise inequality when a logarithm inequality is multiplied by $D(z)$.
Local finiteness and compactness of the disk make all the sums finite.
The bound $\rho \ge 1$ controls the term at $0$, and $\rho < r$ puts the small disk inside the large one.

steps.slogan: Reduce both sums to one finite set $T$ of points.
steps.detail: By local finiteness, the support of $D$ meets the compact disk $\{|z| \le r\}$ in a finite set. Add the point $0$ to get $T$. The disk of radius $\rho$ lies in the disk of radius $r$, so both sides are finite sums over $T$.

steps.slogan: Compare the terms at $z = 0$ using $\rho \ge 1$.
steps.detail: The left side has the term $D(0)\log(r/\rho)$ and the right side has $D(0)\log r$. Since $\rho \ge 1$ gives $\log(r/\rho) \le \log r$ for the [logarithm](c:logarithm), and $D(0) \ge 0$, the left term is at most the right term.

steps.slogan: Compare the terms with $0 < |z| \le \rho$ using $|z| \le \rho$.
steps.detail: Here $|z| \le \rho$ gives $r/\rho \le r/|z|$, so $\log(r/\rho) \le \log(r/|z|)$. Multiplying by $D(z) \ge 0$ keeps the inequality.

steps.slogan: Show that the terms with $\rho < |z| \le r$ are nonnegative on the right.
steps.detail: The left side has no term at such a point $z$. On the right, $|z| \le r$ gives $\log(r/|z|) \ge 0$, and $D(z) \ge 0$, so the term is nonnegative.

steps.slogan: Add the termwise inequalities over $T$ to get the estimate.
steps.detail: Summing over $T$ gives the left side on one side. On the other side it gives $\sum_{z \in T,\, z \ne 0} D(z)\log(r/|z|) + D(0)\log r$, which is $N(D, r)$.

concepts.c:divisor: The function $D$ records multiplicities of points and is the object being counted.
concepts.c:logarithmic-counting-function: The right side is this function, and the proof compares it with a truncated sum.
concepts.c:logarithm: Monotonicity of the logarithm gives each termwise inequality.

source.note: mathlib rewrites both sides as finite sums over one finset and compares them term by term with Real.log_le_log and Finset.sum_le_sum.

statement: Kapranov proposes a [Fourier transform](c:fourier-transform) for noncommutative geometry. It should identify suitable spaces of functions of noncommuting variables with spaces of functions or measures on the space of paths.
conclusion: Under the proposed transform, functions of noncommuting variables correspond to functions or measures on paths.
unknown: The record names a program of Kapranov, which his paper states as an expectation (there should exist such a transform) without hypotheses or a precise theorem, so there is no single mathematical statement to prove.

statement: Let $ABCD$ be a [cyclic quadrilateral](c:cyclic-quadrilateral) whose diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ are perpendicular and meet at $P$. Then the line through $P$ perpendicular to $BC$ passes through the [midpoint](c:midpoint) of $AD$.

hypotheses.text: $ABCD$ is a convex [cyclic quadrilateral](c:cyclic-quadrilateral), with its vertices in this order on a circle.
The diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ are [perpendicular](c:perpendicular-diagonals) and meet at $P$.

conclusion: The perpendicular from $P$ to $BC$ meets $AD$ at its [midpoint](c:midpoint).

proofs.name: Angle chase
proofs.slogan: Show that the perpendicular from $P$ meets $AD$ at a point $M$ with $MA = MP = MD$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for the perpendicular to $BC$; the perpendiculars to the other sides follow by relabeling.

roles.why: A circle through the four vertices gives equal inscribed angles on the arc $DC$.
The right angle at $P$ makes triangles $BPC$ and $APD$ right triangles with complementary acute angles.

steps.slogan: Name the foot $F$ on $BC$ and the point $M$ where the perpendicular meets $AD$.
steps.detail: Triangle $BPC$ has a right angle at $P$, so its angles at $B$ and $C$ are acute and the foot $F$ lies strictly between $B$ and $C$. The ray from $P$ opposite to $PF$ lies inside the vertical angle $APD$, so it meets the segment $AD$ at a point $M$.

steps.slogan: Equate the inscribed angles $\angle DBC$ and $\angle DAC$ on the arc $DC$.
steps.detail: The vertices $A$ and $B$ lie on the same side of line $CD$, so the [inscribed angle](c:inscribed-angle) theorem gives $\angle DBC = \angle DAC$. Call this angle $\theta$.

steps.slogan: Compute $\angle MPD$ from the right triangle $PFB$.
steps.detail: In triangle $PFB$ the angle at $F$ is right and $\angle PBF = \angle DBC = \theta$, so $\angle FPB = 90^\circ - \theta$. Vertical angles give $\angle MPD = \angle FPB = 90^\circ - \theta$.

steps.slogan: Show that $MD = MP$ and $MA = MP$ in the right triangle $APD$.
steps.detail: The [perpendicular diagonals](c:perpendicular-diagonals) make the angle at $P$ in triangle $APD$ right, and $\angle DAP = \theta$. So $\angle ADP = 90^\circ - \theta = \angle MPD$, which gives $MD = MP$. Also $\angle APM = 90^\circ - \angle MPD = \theta = \angle MAP$, so $MA = MP$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two equalities to see that $M$ bisects $AD$.
steps.detail: From $MA = MP = MD$ with $M$ on the segment $AD$, the point $M$ is the [midpoint](c:midpoint) of $AD$.

concepts.c:cyclic-quadrilateral: The common circle gives equal inscribed angles on the arc $DC$.
concepts.c:midpoint: The conclusion is that the perpendicular meets $AD$ at its midpoint.
concepts.c:perpendicular-diagonals: The right angle at $P$ makes the two small triangles right triangles.
concepts.c:inscribed-angle: Equal inscribed angles on one arc link the angles at $A$ and at $B$.

source.note: The standard angle-chasing proof of Brahmagupta's theorem for a cyclic quadrilateral with perpendicular diagonals.

statement: Let $K$ be a finite abelian extension of $\mathbb{Q}$ and $p$ a prime. Then Iwasawa's invariant $\mu$ of the cyclotomic $\mathbb{Z}_p$-extension $K_\infty / K$ is $0$. Equivalently, the exponent of $p$ in the class number of the $n$-th layer is $\lambda n + \nu$ for large $n$, with no $\mu p^n$ term.

hypotheses.text: $K$ is a [number field](c:number-field) that is a finite abelian extension of $\mathbb{Q}$.
$K_\infty / K$ is the cyclotomic $\mathbb{Z}_p$-extension of $K$, inside $K(\zeta_{p^\infty})$.

proofs.name: Vanishing of mu for p-adic L-functions
proofs.slogan: Reduce the vanishing of $\mu$ to the $p$-adic L-functions of Dirichlet characters, then show with equidistribution that their power series are not divisible by $p$.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof; each step rests on the cited paper and on Iwasawa's earlier theory. Sinnott (1984) gives a second proof through the $\Gamma$-transform of a rational function.

roles.why: An abelian field lies in a cyclotomic field, so its class groups split along [Dirichlet characters](c:dirichlet-character) with $p$-adic L-functions.
The cyclotomic $\mathbb{Z}_p$-extension is the tower whose Iwasawa module is linked to the $p$-adic L-functions.

steps.slogan: Reduce the claim to the Iwasawa power series of $p$-adic L-functions.
steps.detail: Iwasawa's theory attaches to each relevant [Dirichlet character](c:dirichlet-character) $\chi$ a power series $f(T, \chi)$ built from the [$p$-adic L-function](c:p-adic-l-function) of $\chi$. Earlier theorems of Iwasawa reduce $\mu(K_\infty / K) = 0$ to $\mu(f(T, \chi)) = 0$ for these series.

steps.slogan: View each power series as the transform of a $p$-adic measure with Bernoulli moments.
steps.detail: The series $f(T, \chi)$ is the $\Gamma$-transform of a $p$-adic measure whose moments are generalized [Bernoulli numbers](c:bernoulli-number). So $\mu = 0$ means that this measure is not divisible by $p$, that is, some value of it is a unit.

steps.slogan: Assume $\mu > 0$ and turn it into congruences modulo $p$ for sums of Bernoulli values.
steps.detail: If $\mu > 0$, the measure vanishes modulo the maximal ideal on every compact open set. The values on cosets modulo $p^n$ are character sums of the first Bernoulli polynomial at fractions $a / (m p^n)$, so every such sum is divisible by the prime.

steps.slogan: Contradict these congruences with an equidistribution argument based on the Weyl criterion.
steps.detail: Ferrero and Washington prove, with the Weyl criterion, an equidistribution result for these fractions. It shows that the character sums cannot all vanish modulo $p$, which contradicts $\mu > 0$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that every power series has $\mu = 0$, and so does $K_\infty / K$.
steps.detail: The contradiction shows $\mu(f(T, \chi)) = 0$ for every relevant character. The reduction of the first step then gives $\mu_p(K_\infty / K) = 0$.

concepts.c:number-field: The theorem concerns class groups of abelian number fields and their cyclotomic towers.
concepts.c:dirichlet-character: Characters split the class groups into pieces tied to $p$-adic L-functions.
concepts.c:p-adic-l-function: Its Iwasawa power series carries the $\mu$-invariant that the proof bounds.
concepts.c:bernoulli-number: Generalized Bernoulli numbers are the moments of the measure behind the series.

source.ref: B. Ferrero and L. C. Washington, The Iwasawa invariant mu_p vanishes for abelian number fields, Annals of Mathematics (2) 109 (1979), no. 2, 377-395
source.note: The paper proves mu = 0 for the Kubota-Leopoldt p-adic L-functions through an equidistribution result, and Iwasawa's earlier theory gives the statement for abelian number fields; Washington, Introduction to Cyclotomic Fields, chapter 7, gives an exposition.

statement: Assume the continuum hypothesis. Let $X$ be a Parovicenko space: a zero-dimensional [compact Hausdorff space](c:compact-hausdorff-space) of weight $\mathfrak{c}$ with no isolated points, in which disjoint open $F_\sigma$ sets have disjoint closures and every nonempty $G_\delta$ set has nonempty interior. Then $X$ is homeomorphic to $\beta\mathbb{N} \setminus \mathbb{N}$.

hypotheses.text: The continuum hypothesis holds, so $\mathfrak{c} = \aleph_1$.
$X$ is a zero-dimensional [compact Hausdorff space](c:compact-hausdorff-space) of weight $\mathfrak{c}$ with no isolated points.
Any two disjoint open $F_\sigma$ subsets of $X$ have disjoint closures.
Every nonempty $G_\delta$ subset of $X$ has nonempty interior.

conclusion: $X$ is [homeomorphic](c:homeomorphism) to $\beta\mathbb{N} \setminus \mathbb{N}$, the remainder of the [Stone-Cech compactification](c:stone-cech-compactification) of $\mathbb{N}$.

proofs.name: Back and forth between Boolean algebras
proofs.slogan: Pass to clopen algebras by Stone duality, then build an isomorphism with $P(\omega)/\mathrm{fin}$ by a back-and-forth argument of length $\omega_1$.
proofs.scope: An outline of Parovicenko's proof. Without the continuum hypothesis the conclusion can fail, because other Parovicenko spaces exist.

roles.why: The hypothesis $\mathfrak{c} = \aleph_1$ lets both algebras be listed in $\omega_1$ steps, each stage countable.
A zero-dimensional [compact Hausdorff space](c:compact-hausdorff-space) is the Stone space of its clopen algebra, and no isolated points makes the algebra atomless.
Disjoint open $F_\sigma$ sets with disjoint closures give the separation property of countable families of clopen sets.
Nonempty interior of $G_\delta$ sets gives nonzero lower bounds for countable families with the finite intersection property.

steps.slogan: Pass from the space to its Boolean algebra of clopen sets by Stone duality.
steps.detail: A zero-dimensional compact Hausdorff space is the Stone space of its [Boolean algebra](c:boolean-algebra) $B$ of clopen sets, and $\beta\mathbb{N} \setminus \mathbb{N}$ is the Stone space of $P(\omega)/\mathrm{fin}$. So $X \cong \beta\mathbb{N} \setminus \mathbb{N}$ exactly when $B \cong P(\omega)/\mathrm{fin}$.

steps.slogan: Translate the axioms on $X$ into properties of the algebra $B$.
steps.detail: No isolated points means that $B$ is atomless, and weight $\mathfrak{c} = \aleph_1$ means $|B| = \aleph_1$. The separation axiom says that countable families $A$ and $C$ of clopen sets, with every member of $A$ disjoint from every member of $C$, are separated by a clopen set. The $G_\delta$ axiom says that a countable family with the finite intersection property has a nonzero lower bound.

steps.slogan: Check that $P(\omega)/\mathrm{fin}$ has the same properties.
steps.detail: It is atomless of size $\mathfrak{c}$, and standard diagonal arguments give the separation property and the lower-bound property. So $\beta\mathbb{N} \setminus \mathbb{N}$ is itself a Parovicenko space.

steps.slogan: Build an isomorphism in $\omega_1$ steps by a back-and-forth argument.
steps.detail: Under the continuum hypothesis, list both algebras in order type $\omega_1$. At a countable stage, extend the partial isomorphism of countable subalgebras by the next element on one side, then on the other. The image of a new element is given by a countable, finitely satisfiable family of conditions, which separation and lower bounds realize; limit stages take unions.

steps.slogan: Take the union of the chain of isomorphisms and dualize it to a homeomorphism.
steps.detail: Every element of both algebras enters at some stage, so the union is an isomorphism $B \to P(\omega)/\mathrm{fin}$. Stone duality turns it into a [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism) $X \to \beta\mathbb{N} \setminus \mathbb{N}$.

concepts.c:compact-hausdorff-space: Compact Hausdorff zero-dimensional spaces are exactly the Stone spaces of Boolean algebras.
concepts.c:homeomorphism: The conclusion and the dualized isomorphism are homeomorphisms.
concepts.c:stone-cech-compactification: The target space is the remainder of this compactification of the integers.
concepts.c:boolean-algebra: The clopen sets form the algebra in which the back-and-forth runs.

source.ref: I. I. Parovicenko, On a universal bicompactum of weight aleph, Doklady Akademii Nauk SSSR 150 (1963), 36-39
source.note: Parovicenko proves that, under the continuum hypothesis, every Parovicenko space is homeomorphic to the remainder of beta N; J. van Mill, An introduction to beta omega, in Handbook of Set-Theoretic Topology (1984), gives an exposition.

statement: The only solutions of the [Diophantine equation](c:diophantine-equation) $x^2 + 7 = 2^n$ in nonnegative integers are $(x, n) = (1, 3), (3, 4), (5, 5), (11, 7), (181, 15)$.

hypotheses.text: The unknowns $x$ and $n$ are nonnegative integers.

proofs.name: Factorization and 2-adic analysis
proofs.slogan: Factor in the ring of integers of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-7})$ to reach a Lucas sequence, then solve $U_m = \pm 1$ by 2-adic analysis.
proofs.scope: An outline in which steps 1 to 4 are complete arguments and step 5 rests on the cited papers. The list is complete for $x \ge 0$.

roles.why: Integrality of $x$ and $n$ gives the parity argument and the factorization in a ring of integers.

steps.slogan: Reduce to $n \ge 3$ and odd $x$.
steps.detail: For $n \le 2$ the number $2^n - 7$ is negative, so there is no solution. For $n \ge 3$, $x^2 = 2^n - 7 \equiv 1 \pmod 8$, so $x$ is odd.

steps.slogan: Factor $x^2 + 7$ in the ring $\mathbb{Z}[\alpha]$ with $\alpha = (1 + \sqrt{-7})/2$.
steps.detail: The ring $\mathbb{Z}[\alpha]$ is the [ring of integers](c:ring-of-integers) of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-7})$ and is a [Euclidean domain](c:euclidean-domain), so factorization into primes is [unique](c:unique-factorization) up to the units $\pm 1$. For $u = (x + \sqrt{-7})/2$ we get $u\bar u = 2^{n-2}$, and $2 = \alpha\bar\alpha$ with $\alpha$ and $\bar\alpha$ non-associate primes.

steps.slogan: Show that $u$ is $\pm\alpha^{m}$ or $\pm\bar\alpha^{m}$, where $m = n - 2$.
steps.detail: If $\alpha$ divided both $u$ and $\bar u$, it would divide $u - \bar u = \sqrt{-7}$, whose norm $7$ is not divisible by $2$. So the $m$ factors $\alpha$ of $u\bar u = \alpha^m\bar\alpha^m$ all lie in $u$ or all lie in $\bar u$, and the factors $\bar\alpha$ lie in the other one. Hence $u = \pm\alpha^m$ or $u = \pm\bar\alpha^m$.

steps.slogan: Compare $u - \bar u = \sqrt{-7}$ with the powers of $\alpha$ to get $U_m = \pm 1$.
steps.detail: Put $U_k = (\alpha^k - \bar\alpha^k)/(\alpha - \bar\alpha)$; this integer sequence has $U_0 = 0$, $U_1 = 1$ and $U_{k+1} = U_k - 2U_{k-1}$. Since $u - \bar u = \alpha - \bar\alpha$, both cases of the last step give $U_m = \pm 1$. They also give $x = |\alpha^m + \bar\alpha^m|$.

steps.slogan: Solve $U_m = \pm 1$ in integers $m \ge 0$ by 2-adic analysis, as in the cited papers.
steps.detail: The cited proofs study $U_m$ in the 2-adic integers, where exactly one of $\alpha$, $\bar\alpha$ is a unit and the other has [2-adic valuation](c:2-adic-valuation) $1$. Congruences modulo powers of $2$ restrict $m$ to a thin set of residue classes, and a final argument excludes every $m$ beyond $13$. The result is that $U_m = \pm 1$ holds only for $m = 1, 2, 3, 5, 13$.

steps.slogan: Convert the five values of $m$ back to the solutions $(x, n)$.
steps.detail: Take $n = m + 2$ and $x = |\alpha^m + \bar\alpha^m|$. The values $m = 1, 2, 3, 5, 13$ give $(x, n) = (1, 3), (3, 4), (5, 5), (11, 7), (181, 15)$, and each satisfies $x^2 + 7 = 2^n$.

concepts.c:diophantine-equation: The problem is to find all integer solutions of one exponential equation.
concepts.c:ring-of-integers: The factorization takes place in the ring of integers of a quadratic field.
concepts.c:euclidean-domain: The norm makes the ring Euclidean, which gives unique factorization.
concepts.c:unique-factorization: Unique factorization splits the powers of $2$ between $u$ and its conjugate.
concepts.c:2-adic-valuation: The valuations of $\alpha$ and $\bar\alpha$ drive the 2-adic analysis.

source.ref: T. Nagell, The diophantine equation x^2 + 7 = 2^n, Arkiv for Matematik 4 (1961), 185-187; see also Th. Skolem, S. Chowla and D. J. Lewis, The diophantine equation 2^(n+2) - 7 = x^2 and related problems, Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society 10 (1959), 663-669
source.note: Ramanujan conjectured the list in 1913 and Nagell proved it in 1948; steps 1 to 4 are the factorization argument, and step 5 is the 2-adic part of the cited proofs.

statement: Let $G$ be a [finite simple group](c:finite-simple-group) of [characteristic 2 type](c:characteristic-2-type) whose 2-local rank $e(G)$ is at least $3$. Then $G$ is of $\mathrm{GF}(2)$-type, or of standard type for an odd prime, or of uniqueness type.

hypotheses.text: $G$ is a [finite simple group](c:finite-simple-group).
$G$ is of [characteristic 2 type](c:characteristic-2-type): $F^*(H) = O_2(H)$ for every 2-local subgroup $H$.
The 2-local rank $e(G)$ is at least $3$: some odd prime $p$ has a 2-local subgroup that holds an elementary abelian $p$-subgroup of rank $3$.

conclusion: $G$ is of $\mathrm{GF}(2)$-type, of standard type for an odd prime, or of uniqueness type.

proofs.name: Local analysis with signalizer functors
proofs.slogan: Study the 2-local subgroups that normalize a rank 3 odd $p$-subgroup with signalizer functors, and sort the outcomes into three types.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof, with rank $3$ proved by Aschbacher and rank at least $4$ by Gorenstein and Lyons. Each step rests on the cited work; that no simple group has uniqueness type is a separate theorem of Aschbacher.

roles.why: Simplicity makes every proper normal subgroup trivial, so a local subgroup cannot hide a normal structure of $G$.
Every 2-local subgroup is controlled by its 2-core $O_2(H)$, which gives a uniform local structure.
A rank 3 odd $p$-subgroup $A$ inside a 2-local subgroup is the object whose invariant 2-locals the proof studies.

steps.slogan: Fix an odd prime $p$ and a rank 3 elementary abelian $p$-subgroup $A$ of a 2-local subgroup.
steps.detail: The hypothesis $e(G) \ge 3$ gives such $p$ and $A$. Characteristic 2 type says that each 2-local subgroup $H$ of the [finite simple group](c:finite-simple-group) $G$ has $F^*(H) = O_2(H)$, so $H$ is determined by its 2-core.

steps.slogan: Apply signalizer functor theory to the 2-local subgroups that $A$ normalizes.
steps.detail: The cited work studies the $A$-invariant 2-local subgroups and uses signalizer functor theory to control the centralizers $C_G(a)$ for $a \in A$ and the subgroups that these 2-locals generate.

steps.slogan: Separate the case where the relevant 2-locals lie in one maximal 2-local subgroup.
steps.detail: If the 2-local subgroups through a suitable subgroup all lie in a single maximal 2-local subgroup, $G$ has uniqueness type, which is one of the three conclusions.

steps.slogan: Analyze pairs of distinct maximal 2-locals to find a standard component or a GF(2) structure.
steps.detail: If no unique maximal 2-local exists, the cited work shows that either $G$ is of standard type for an odd prime, through a standard component in a centralizer, or $G$ satisfies the structural conditions of $\mathrm{GF}(2)$-type.

steps.slogan: Combine the three outcomes to get the trichotomy.
steps.detail: Every case of the analysis ends in one of the three types, so $G$ is of $\mathrm{GF}(2)$-type, of standard type for an odd prime, or of uniqueness type.

concepts.c:finite-simple-group: Simplicity keeps local subgroups from hiding a normal structure.
concepts.c:characteristic-2-type: This hypothesis makes every 2-local subgroup controlled by its 2-core.

source.ref: D. Gorenstein and R. Lyons, The local structure of finite groups of characteristic 2 type, Memoirs of the American Mathematical Society 42 (1983), no. 276; M. Aschbacher, Finite groups of rank 3, I, Inventiones Mathematicae 63 (1981), and II, Inventiones Mathematicae 71 (1983)
source.note: Gorenstein and Lyons treat e(G) at least 4 and Aschbacher treats e(G) = 3; the steps outline the local analysis that both works carry out.

statement: On each side of a convex [quadrilateral](c:quadrilateral) $ABCD$ build a [square](c:square) outward. Let $P$, $Q$, $R$, $S$ be the centers of the squares on $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, $DA$. Then the segments $PR$ and $QS$ have equal length and are perpendicular.

hypotheses.text: $ABCD$ is a convex [quadrilateral](c:quadrilateral).
A [square](c:square) is built outward on each of the four sides.

proofs.name: Complex numbers
proofs.slogan: Write the four centers as complex numbers and show that $s - q$ equals $i(r - p)$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. In the degenerate case $r = p$, both vectors $r - p$ and $s - q$ are zero.

roles.why: Convexity lets the vertices run counterclockwise, so outward is the same side, to the right, of every directed side.
Each outward square fixes its center as the midpoint of the side plus a right-turned half side.

steps.slogan: Place the vertices as [complex numbers](c:complex-number) $a, b, c, d$ in counterclockwise order.
steps.detail: After relabeling, the convex quadrilateral runs counterclockwise. Multiplication by $i$ is the [rotation](c:rotation) by $90^\circ$ about $0$, and multiplication by $-i$ is the rotation by $-90^\circ$.

steps.slogan: Write the center of each outward square.
steps.detail: The outward square on $AB$ lies to the right of the directed side $a \to b$. Its center is the midpoint plus half the side vector turned by $-90^\circ$, so $p = \frac{a+b}{2} - i\,\frac{b-a}{2} = \frac{(1+i)a + (1-i)b}{2}$. Likewise $q$, $r$, $s$ come from the pairs $(b, c)$, $(c, d)$, $(d, a)$.

steps.slogan: Compute the vectors $r - p$ and $s - q$.
steps.detail: Subtract the formulas for the centers and group the terms by $c - a$ and $d - b$. This gives $r - p = \frac{(1+i)(c-a) + (1-i)(d-b)}{2}$ and $s - q = \frac{(1+i)(d-b) - (1-i)(c-a)}{2}$.

steps.slogan: Show that $s - q = i(r - p)$.
steps.detail: Multiplying $r - p$ by $i$ gives $\frac{(i-1)(c-a) + (i+1)(d-b)}{2}$. Since $i - 1 = -(1-i)$ and $i + 1 = 1 + i$, this equals $s - q$.

steps.slogan: Read off equal lengths and a right angle between $PR$ and $QS$.
steps.detail: Rotation by $90^\circ$ keeps lengths and turns the vector $PR$ into the vector $QS$. So $|QS| = |PR|$ and $QS \perp PR$.

concepts.c:quadrilateral: The four vertices of the quadrilateral become four complex numbers in counterclockwise order.
concepts.c:square: Each outward square contributes its center as a formula in the two end vertices.
concepts.c:complex-number: Complex numbers turn rotation by $90^\circ$ into multiplication by $i$.
concepts.c:rotation: The relation $s - q = i(r - p)$ says that one segment is a rotation of the other.

source.note: The standard proof of van Aubel's theorem with complex numbers.

statement: Let $G$ be a finite group of even order that equals its [commutator subgroup](c:commutator-subgroup), such that any two [cyclic subgroups](c:cyclic-group) of even order that meet nontrivially lie in a common cyclic subgroup. Then $G \cong \mathrm{PSL}(2, q)$ for some prime power $q \ge 4$.

hypotheses.text: $G$ is a finite group of even order.
If $I$ and $J$ are [cyclic subgroups](c:cyclic-group) of $G$ of even order with $I \cap J \ne 1$, then some cyclic subgroup of $G$ contains both.
$G$ equals its [commutator subgroup](c:commutator-subgroup).

conclusion: $G$ is isomorphic to the [projective special linear group](c:projective-linear-group) $\mathrm{PSL}(2, q)$ over the [finite field](c:finite-field) with $q \ge 4$ elements.

proofs.name: Cyclic intersections and characters
proofs.slogan: Turn the cyclic condition into trivial intersections of maximal cyclic subgroups, then use character theory to identify the group.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof; steps 2 to 4 rest on the cited paper. Steps 1 and 4 are exact for the stated hypotheses.

roles.why: Even order gives involutions, around which the local structure of $G$ is built.
The condition forces maximal cyclic subgroups of even order to meet pairwise trivially.
Perfectness rules out the solvable and non-perfect groups that also satisfy the cyclic condition.

steps.slogan: Show that distinct maximal cyclic subgroups of even order meet trivially.
steps.detail: Let $I$ and $J$ be maximal among the [cyclic subgroups](c:cyclic-group) of even order, with $I \cap J \ne 1$. Some cyclic subgroup $K$ contains both, so maximality gives $I = K = J$.

steps.slogan: Determine the 2-local structure: the Sylow 2-subgroups and the centralizers of involutions.
steps.detail: The cited paper uses the trivial intersection property and even order to show that the [Sylow 2-subgroups](c:sylow-subgroup) are dihedral or elementary abelian and to fix the structure of the normalizers of the maximal cyclic subgroups of even order.

steps.slogan: Compute the order and the class structure of $G$ with Brauer's character theory.
steps.detail: The cited paper applies the character theory of groups with trivial intersection cyclic subgroups, in the style of Brauer's exceptional characters, to find the order of $G$ and the sizes of its conjugacy classes.

steps.slogan: Identify $G$ with $\mathrm{PSL}(2, q)$ using that $G$ is perfect.
steps.detail: The data of the previous steps agree with those of $\mathrm{PSL}(2, q)$, and the cited paper concludes $G \cong \mathrm{PSL}(2, q)$. Perfectness excludes the groups with these properties that are not perfect, such as dihedral groups and $A_4$.

concepts.c:cyclic-group: The hypothesis is a condition on how cyclic subgroups of even order intersect.
concepts.c:commutator-subgroup: Perfectness means that the commutator subgroup is the whole group.
concepts.c:sylow-subgroup: The Sylow 2-subgroups fix the 2-local structure of the group.
concepts.c:projective-linear-group: The group $\mathrm{PSL}(2, q)$ is the conclusion of the characterization.
concepts.c:finite-field: The parameter $q$ is the size of a finite field.

source.ref: R. Brauer, M. Suzuki and G. E. Wall, A characterization of the one-dimensional unimodular projective groups over finite fields, Illinois Journal of Mathematics 2 (1958), 718-745
source.note: The paper characterizes the groups LF(2, q) by exactly these three conditions.
